title: VLAN Hopping: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: You're only supposed to reach your own floor. But a clever attacker can sneak into someone else's. This is called V L A N hopping.

scenes.heading: The hotel keycard mix-up
scenes.narration: Think of a hotel where each floor is a V L A N, and the lift is a trunk. In a switch spoofing attack, a guest pretends to be hotel staff. They flash a fake master keycard, using D T P, and the lift treats them like a trunk. Suddenly they can reach every floor. In double tagging, the guest stacks two stickers on a letter. The first lift removes one, and the second delivers to a floor they shouldn't reach.

scenes.heading: How to stop it
scenes.narration: The fixes are simple. Turn off D T P on access ports. Set unused ports to access mode and shut them down. And change the native V L A N to one nobody uses.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. D T P isn't a security feature. It's the thing attackers abuse. Double tagging can cross several switches if the native V L A N matches. And port security doesn't stop it, because it limits M A C addresses, not trunking.

items.right: It can be abused to form trunks
It limits MACs, not trunk negotiation

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva VLAN hopping lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Switch spoofing abuses D T P, and double tagging abuses the native V L A N. Turn D T P off on access ports. And move the native V L A N away from V L A N one. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva VLAN hopping lab.

points.t: Spoofing abuses DTP; double tagging abuses native VLAN
